summary: Describes AES-CMAC-PRF-128, a pseudo-random function based on AES for IPsec implementations that want to use AES for IKE. It supports fixed and variable key sizes. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: IKE needs a mixing recipe that turns secrets into random-looking values. This gives a recipe built from AES.

questions: how does ikev2 use aes-cmac as a prf
how does aes-cmac-prf-128 handle keys that are not 128 bits
what is the iana value for prf_aes128_cmac
subtitle: A pseudo-random function built on AES-CMAC that lets IKEv2 use AES with keys of any length.

tldr.problem: Some IPsec implementations want a pseudo-random function (PRF) based on AES for IKEv2, but AES-CMAC accepts only 128-bit keys while IKEv2 sometimes needs variable-length keys.
tldr.mechanism: AES-CMAC-PRF-128 uses a 128-bit key as it is, and turns any other key length into a 128-bit key by running AES-CMAC with an all-zero key over it. It then applies AES-CMAC with that key to the message.
tldr.outcome: IKEv2 can use AES-CMAC for keying material and for authentication with shared secrets of any length. IANA allocated value 8 for it.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 4615 as a Proposed Standard, published in August 2006, with no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a New PRF for IKEv2
sections.content:
RFC 4493 describes how to use the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) as a Message Authentication Code with a 128-bit output. That 128-bit output is useful as a long-lived pseudo-random function (PRF).

This document specifies a PRF that supports fixed and variable key sizes, for use in the key derivation function and for authentication in IKEv2 (RFC 4306). It is meant for IPsec implementations that want an AES-based PRF.
sections.eli5: IKE needs a mixing recipe that turns secrets into random-looking values. This one is built from AES.

sections.title: Fixed and Variable Key Sizes
sections.content:
AES-CMAC-PRF-128 is identical to AES-CMAC from RFC 4493, except that the 128-bit key length restriction is removed. The RFC names the variable-length key VK.

IKEv2 uses PRFs for several purposes, mainly generating keying material and authenticating the IKE_SA, and it distinguishes PRFs with fixed key sizes from those with variable key sizes. AES-CMAC-PRF-128 is treated as taking fixed-size keys of 16 octets when generating keying material, but variable key sizes for authentication.

When generating keying material, half the bits must come from Ni and half from Nr, taking the first bits of each. When authenticating with shared secrets, the secret does not have to be 16 octets long.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the recipe wants a key of one exact size. Other times, like with a password you picked, the key can be any length, and the recipe has to cope.

sections.title: The Algorithm
sections.content:
The inputs are the variable-length key VK, the message M, and their lengths in octets, VKlen and len. The output is PRV, a 128-bit pseudo-random value. A working variable K is a 128-bit key for AES-CMAC.

  • Step 1: if VKlen is 16, then K := VK. Otherwise K := AES-CMAC(0^128, VK, VKlen), which uses the 128-bit all-zero string as the key and VK as the message.
  • Step 2: PRV := AES-CMAC(K, M, len), and return PRV.

So a key of exactly 128 bits is used as it is, and a key that is longer or shorter is first turned into a 128-bit key.
sections.eli5: If your key already fits, use it. If not, run it through a squisher that always gives the right size, then do the real mixing.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
The RFC gives three test cases, all with the same 20-octet message, so implementers can check their code. They use a key of 18 octets, one of 16 octets and one of 10 octets, which exercise both branches of step 1.

For the 16-octet key 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f, the expected output is 980ae87b5f4c9c5214f5b6a8455e4c2d.
sections.eli5: These are practice problems with the answers in the back of the book, so you can check that your recipe works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of AES-CMAC-PRF-128 rests on the strength of AES and AES-CMAC. At the time of writing, the RFC says there were no known practical cryptographic attacks against either. Part of the strength also lies in the secret key VK and in correct implementations. VK needs to be chosen independently and randomly, based on RFC 4086, and both VK and K should be kept safe and periodically refreshed.

If VK is longer than 128 bits and is shortened to fit, some entropy might be lost, but K keeps about 128 bits of entropy. The RFC recommends VK of at least 128 bits and discourages VK of 64 bits or fewer, because of the small entropy.
sections.eli5: A good lock needs a good key. Pick a long, truly random key, keep it safe and swap it now and then.

sections.title: IANA Allocation
sections.content: IANA allocated the value 8 for IKEv2 Transform Type 2 (Pseudo-Random Function) to the PRF_AES128_CMAC algorithm. That is the number two IKEv2 peers use to agree on this PRF.
sections.eli5: The algorithm got its own number, 8, so two computers can say which recipe they mean.
